audience: AI engineers evaluating open-weight frontier models for coding/agentic tasks

title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
why: If you ship a web map, swapping earcut for this ISC-licensed drop-in cut triangulation of 3.74M polygons from 557 ms to 489 ms natively and 1.4-2.1x in the browser, with the same API and triangle output.
notes: earstrip is one C++ header plus a WebAssembly/npm build that takes earcut's arguments; self-reported 14% faster than earcut.hpp 3.2.4 natively and 1.4-2.1x faster than earcut.js 3.2.4 in-browser, depending on call path (direct calls, all polygons in one call, hit the 2.1x figure in JavaScriptCore).

The engine replaced a constrained Delaunay triangulator (2.93s on 3.74M Masovian zoom-13 polygons, one M4 Pro core) with ear clipping, reaching 489ms; each optimization is a separate commit timed on the same data.

Load-bearing optimizations, in order of savings: test only reflex vertices (dents) not all points; skip convex polygons entirely; emit triangle strips (35.8M indices vs 64.5M); bucket dents along the bounding box for large polygons; a branchless counting pass (min of three determinants >= 0 means inside) before the exact dent loop.

Holes are bridged via David Eberly's method (ray from the rightmost hole vertex, bridge to the triangle's safe endpoint); polygons with >=128 rings fall back to Delaunay because bridge-finding scans the whole boundary each time (a world-map polygon with 11,675 holes takes earstrip 606ms vs Delaunay 17ms).

Grid rounding can destroy the simple-polygon precondition of Meisters' 1975 theorem; when no ear is found, earstrip drops zero-area corners and retries, then falls back to Delaunay (76 polygons in the older Masovian build); the map generator now uses GEOS snap rounding so a fresh build cuts every polygon.

Accuracy claim: on polygons ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles diverge from an even-odd fill on 31% of pixels on average versus earstrip's 0.15%; WASM builds match native triangle output on all 4.4M zoom-13/9 polygons.
summary: earstrip is an ISC-licensed polygon triangulator extracted from a map engine, shipped as a single C++ header and a WebAssembly/npm build with an earcut-compatible API. The author replaced a constrained Delaunay triangulator (2.93s on 3.74M Masovian Voivodeship zoom-13 polygons on one M4 Pro core) with ear clipping and rebuilt it one commit at a time, reaching 489ms native, reportedly 14% faster than earcut.hpp and 1.4-2.1x faster than earcut.js in the browser. Key wins come from testing only reflex vertices (dents), skipping convex polygons, emitting triangle strips, bucketing dents for large rings, and a branchless counting pass before the exact inside-triangle check. Holes are opened with Eberly-style bridges, and polygons with >=128 rings or that defeat ear clipping (grid rounding can break the simple-polygon assumption behind Meisters' 1975 two-ears theorem) fall back to the retained Delaunay code. The author reports earstrip's triangles diverge from an even-odd fill on 0.15% of pixels versus earcut's 31% on hard cases, and notes earcut.hpp loses most of its speed in its ear-search loop when compiled to WASM. All benchmark numbers are self-reported, with repository, polygons, and timing code published.
novelty: ear-clipping triangulator beats earcut via incremental optimization, open-sourced
audience: graphics/mapping engineers and computational geometry practitioners

title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
why: If your SSH or CI configs use passwords and accept-new host key handling, a single hostile Tor exit node can pin its own key on first connection, steal your password, and backdoor the server with no warning ever firing.
notes: 333 Tor exit nodes were compromised at once, more than 10% of the roughly 3,000-node network, and routed through 12 SSH interception servers run by the attacker.

When a user ignored the SSH host key change warning, the attacker did three things: stole the SSH password, opened a connection to the real server to observe every typed command (MITM), and opened a second connection to install Ebury, an SSH credential-harvesting malware active for over a decade.

The core weakness is TOFU: trust-on-first-use only protects from the second connection onward, so a first connection through a hostile exit lets the attacker present its own key and get it pinned with no warning. Key-based auth would still allow session interception but not arbitrary new sessions, since the private key is not exposed.
In parallel, the attacker blocked ports used for encrypted email while leaving unencrypted email ports open, betting that some clients or services would downgrade to plaintext.

Volunteer researcher Kaba found the campaign by scripting a poll of all ~3,000 exit nodes against a test server to detect SSH fingerprint mismatches, then ran a honeypot to watch the interception software log in and install Ebury.

One open question flagged in the discussion: the attacker reached a second Tor server (Switzerland2) over SSH using an RSA key investigators could not find in that server's authorized_keys, with no stated explanation; the Lemmy thread is commentary, not a vendor or first-party writeup.
summary: A reported campaign hijacked 333 Tor exit nodes, over 10% of the ~3,000-node network, to run SSH man-in-the-middle attacks. When a user ignored an SSH host key change warning, the attacker stole the password, relayed the session to observe typed commands, and opened a second connection to infect the server with Ebury, a long-running SSH credential-harvesting malware. The attack exploits trust-on-first-use, which offers no protection on a first connection through a hostile node, a gap worsened by tooling defaults like disabled strict host key checking and accept-new. The attacker also blocked encrypted email ports while leaving plaintext ports open, hoping clients would downgrade. Volunteer researcher Kaba detected it by polling all exit nodes for SSH fingerprint mismatches against a test server and running a honeypot. The piece is a discussion thread summarizing the event; recommended defenses are key-based SSH auth over passwords and rejecting unencrypted email, and one unexplained detail is the attacker's access to a second Tor server via an RSA key not found in its authorized_keys.
novelty: 333 Tor exit nodes (10%+ of network) hijacked en masse for SSH MITM
audience: security engineers and anyone using Tor/SSH over untrusted networks

title: Speeding up code review with `small-change`
why: If AI-assisted coding is raising your team's merge rate, human PR review becomes the bottleneck Larson describes: his p50 review time doubled from 33 to 77 minutes in two years, and this is a concrete recipe for routing low-risk PRs around human review without dropping quality.
notes: Self-reported metrics from Imprint: average engineer merges 4x more PRs than two years ago, two teams at 10x, one engineer at 25x the old average; p50 review time rose from ~33 to ~77 min, correlated with merge volume.

Quality claim (no methodology given): incidents down 42% half-over-half, critical incidents down 78% half-over-half despite higher velocity, which Larson offers as evidence the velocity/quality tradeoff is a false construct.

small-change eligibility is a non-human-modifiable GitHub check, all criteria required: <1,000 LOC, zero p1/p2 findings from the ai-code-review bot, author has 10+ prior merged PRs in that service's directories, impacts fewer than N services (N=1 frontend monorepo, N=3 backend), excludes shared libs/utils; per-path .small_change file can exclude areas like money movement.

The review-small-change skill can only approve or ignore, never comment, deliberately avoiding 'meat proxy review': harness-generated comments that get answered by harnesses, turning review into theater. Sensitive topics (payments, security) still trip a flag to human review.
Social contract: any incident from an auto-approved small-change is treated as a system failure to be fixed at the CICD/verification/harness level, not blamed on a reviewer.

Early and explicitly inconclusive: only ~10% of changes currently qualify; success hinges on expanding verification coverage, which Larson notes is harder in low-scale-complexity, high-domain-complexity software than in high-scale products where incremental rollouts give more coverage. Separately mentions 'fleet', a centrally orchestrated harness akin to Stripe's Minions.
summary: Will Larson describes Imprint's 'small-change' mechanism for cutting code-review load as AI-assisted development pushes merge volume up (self-reported: 4x average, up to 25x for one engineer) and drove p50 review time from ~33 to ~77 minutes. A CICD-managed GitHub check marks a PR as a small-change when it meets all criteria: under 1,000 LOC, no p1/p2 findings from their ai-code-review bot, author has 10+ prior merges in the affected service, fewer than N services touched (1 on frontend, 3 on backend), and no shared-library files; per-path .small_change files allow exclusions like money-movement code. Qualifying PRs can be auto-approved by a 'review-small-change' skill that only approves or ignores and never comments, a design choice meant to avoid 'meat proxy review' where harness-generated comments are answered by harnesses. Errors from auto-approved changes are treated as system failures to be fixed in verification tooling rather than reviewer mistakes. Larson calls results too early to judge: about 10% of changes currently qualify, and the approach's success depends on expanding verification coverage, which he argues is harder for high-domain-complexity software. He frames all four traditional reasons for review (knowledge sharing, error prevention, malicious-behavior prevention, compliance) as better served by other mechanisms, and reports incidents down 42% and critical incidents down 78% half-over-half, without stated methodology.
novelty: CICD-gated auto-approval tier for low-risk PRs, no human review
audience: eng leaders and platform teams designing AI-era code review processes

title: Show HN: Run full iOS 16.5 firmware on Android Devices
why: An unmodified iOS 16.5 userland now reaches the SpringBoard home screen on a $300 Snapdragon Android phone with no Apple binaries modified, proving the whole stack can be driven by replacement drivers and an injected library rather than Apple silicon.
notes: Boots Apple's open-source XNU (xnu-8796.121.2, the iOS 16.5 kernel) under a custom EFI loader and a Mu-Silicium UEFI port, then runs the stock launchd to backboardd to SpringBoard chain unchanged; the iOS frameworks and dyld shared cache are not altered by a byte, with missing pieces supplied by driver replacements or a library injected via DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES.

Runs two ways: on a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) entirely in RAM via fastboot boot with nothing flashed, so a reboot returns to Android; or in QEMU virt aarch64 with no phone. Reaches the lock screen in about 20 seconds on hardware (2 to 3 minutes in QEMU).

Working on-device: Goodix GT9916 multitouch, Wi-Fi over ath11k/WCN6750 at a self-reported 55 to 90 Mbit/s, Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno (OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation), speaker/mic audio, camera with HEIC capture, up to 8 cores at 2.4 GHz, and Sileo plus Procursus (dpkg/apt) with SSH.

Not working: cellular, Bluetooth, charging under the custom kernel (the phone only discharges), and App Store/Apple ID because there is no Secure Enclave and the FairPlay daemon exits. Metal for apps is partial, with 293 of 456 system shaders running on the Adreno.

No Apple files ship in the repos: ios165/fetch.sh pulls a 7.4 GB iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's CDN on the user's machine, and the phone's own GPU/Wi-Fi/audio/haptic firmware is pulled from the device's Android partitions rather than redistributed. The XNU fork is distributed under APSL 2.0.

The authors call it a research bench, not a ROM: sessions are time-limited (for example 900 seconds) and then the kernel hands control and its log back to the resident loader. Project credited to OOSEX GANG; not affiliated with or endorsed by Apple.
summary: HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel (xnu-8796.121.2, from iOS 16.5) on non-Apple hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space, from launchd through SpringBoard, on top of it. It uses a custom EFI loader, a Mu-Silicium UEFI port, replacements for Apple's closed drivers (IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack), minicrypto in place of corecrypto, and AMFI/Sandbox stand-ins; iOS binaries are untouched, with gaps filled by driver replacements or a library injected via DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES. It runs on a POCO X5 Pro 5G (Snapdragon 778G) entirely in RAM via fastboot boot, leaving Android intact after reboot, or in QEMU aarch64. Touchscreen, Wi-Fi (ath11k/WCN6750, a claimed 55 to 90 Mbit/s), Adreno 642L GPU via Mesa/freedreno, audio, camera, and Sileo/Procursus jailbreak tooling work; cellular, Bluetooth, charging, full Metal (293 of 456 shaders), and App Store/Apple ID (no Secure Enclave, FairPlay daemon exits) do not. No Apple files are redistributed: the IPSW is fetched from Apple's CDN and vendor firmware is pulled from the phone's own Android partitions. The authors describe it as a time-limited research bench that returns control to the loader, not a usable ROM.
novelty: unmodified iOS 16.5 userland booted on Android hardware via custom EFI/UEFI loader and drivers
audience: low-level systems/kernel and mobile security researchers

title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France
why: If you run 9.9.9.9 for threat filtering, DNS from your French networks stops resolving on November 24, 2026, and the ruling establishes that a single national court can order a passive resolver to lie about DNS answers.
notes: A French court ruled for beIN, a Qatari-owned company with French offices, ordering Quad9 to stop recursive DNS resolution for domains beIN says infringe its sports-broadcast rights; the per-day penalty was cut from EUR 580,000 to EUR 1,000.

Quad9 is a Swiss nonprofit foundation that is free, requires no sign-up or identity, and keeps no user-to-jurisdiction mapping, so it argues it cannot reliably identify French users to apply geo-scoped blocking without abandoning its no-logging privacy stance.

It rejected the technically viable workaround: adding the names to the global malicious-domain list used by 9.9.9.9 (but not the non-filtering 9.9.9.10). Quad9 says that would impose a French ruling on every user worldwide for one private company's benefit.

Precedent cited: in a 2021-2023 German case, Quad9 tried geoIP blocking as a stopgap, Sony Music used a VPN to reach the blocked content from Germany, and the court fined Quad9 for noncompliance. Quad9 says it eventually won but spent years and six figures.

Quad9 says roughly 20 other similar suits are pending against it (and other resolver operators) in France and that accumulating penalties would threaten its survival; its departure is framed as principle, not just finances. An appeal is pending.

The post lists French networks that will lose service, including DINUM, RENATER, Institut Pasteur, EDF, SNCF, France Televisions, Thales, Dassault Systemes, and IDEMIA; Quad9 notes AS numbers are not reliable jurisdictional identifiers.
summary: Quad9, a Swiss nonprofit recursive DNS resolver, says a French court ruled against it in a suit by beIN, ordering it to block DNS resolution for domains beIN claims infringe its sports-broadcast copyrights, with the penalty reduced from EUR 580,000 to EUR 1,000 per day. Rather than comply, Quad9 will withdraw all service from France on November 24, 2026, after nearly nine years of operation. It argues compliance is impossible or unacceptable on three grounds: it keeps no user database or jurisdiction mapping, so per-country blocking would require logging it refuses to do; geoIP blocking is defeatable by VPN and already produced a contempt fine in a 2021-2023 German case brought by Sony Music; and global blocking (on the filtering 9.9.9.9 resolvers) would extend a French ruling to all users worldwide. Quad9 says it faces about 20 other pending French cases and cannot absorb cumulative penalties, that DNS blocking does not remove infringing content, and that an appeal is pending. The post lists French government, research, utility, transport, health, and industry networks that will lose service, and urges French users to lobby legislators and the regulator ARCOM.
novelty: Quad9 withdraws from France rather than block DNS for copyright case
audience: security engineers, privacy advocates, DNS/infra operators, internet policy watchers

title: OpenShell – A safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents
why: If you run coding agents that need real credentials and shell access, this is a per-sandbox way to inject secrets only for approved endpoints and to gate policy expansions behind a verifier before an agent reaches a new host or API.
notes: NVIDIA open-source project (Apache 2.0); the 0.1.x line adds a stated stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs.

Enforcement is kernel-level: each agent runs in an isolated sandbox where kernel controls confine file access and syscalls, and every outbound network connection passes a policy check before leaving the sandbox.
Credential handling: agents never see real credentials; OpenShell injects them only into requests bound for approved endpoints, including inference providers.

Policy changes go through formal verification that flags newly granted risky access (reaching a new host with credentials, calling a new API method) and holds those changes for human review before approval.

Runs on Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and Windows via WSL 2 (experimental), with Docker, Podman, or host virtualization; Kubernetes deploy via Helm requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy. SDKs ship for Python, TypeScript, Go, and Rust.

No independent benchmarks or third-party security evaluation in the text; the formal-verification and isolation claims are the project's own. Anonymous operational telemetry is on by default and can be disabled or compiled out.
summary: OpenShell is an NVIDIA open-source runtime (Apache 2.0) for running fleets of autonomous AI agents under declared policies. It governs agents two ways: kernel-level instrumentation enforces policy on every file access, syscall, and network connection within a per-agent sandbox, and formal verification checks what a proposed policy change would allow before it is applied, flagging risky new access such as a new host reached with credentials or a new API method for human review. Agents never handle real credentials; the gateway injects them only for approved endpoints, including inference. The architecture splits into a gateway control plane, a supervisor, and sandboxes; it supports Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, and experimental Windows WSL 2, and deploys via Docker, Podman, or Kubernetes with Helm (requiring a NetworkPolicy-enforcing CNI). SDKs exist for Python, TypeScript, Go, and Rust, plus installable CLI skills for coding agents. The isolation and verification claims are the project's own; the README includes no independent benchmarks or security audits, and anonymous operational telemetry is enabled by default.
novelty: kernel-enforced sandboxing plus formal verification of agent policy changes
audience: engineers deploying autonomous coding/agent fleets who need credential and access isolation

title: Benchmarking Bot Detection Systems Against Modern AI Agents in 2026
why: If you rely on hCaptcha, Turnstile, or Cloudflare Bot Management to keep LLM browsing agents off your endpoints, this benchmark reports they catch 9-44% of agent sessions: vision-capable agents driving genuine browsers defeat the device-fingerprint and puzzle defenses that still reliably stop scripted bots.
notes: Vendor-run benchmark: the authors work at Proof of Human, PBC, and Proof of Human was the top scorer (99% aggregate detection), so treat the headline ranking as a self-reported claim, not an independent evaluation.
Aggregate detection rates across all adversaries: Proof of Human 99%, Google reCAPTCHA v3 69.4%, hCaptcha 44.3%, Cloudflare Turnstile 42.1%, Cloudflare Bot Management 9.1%.

The split is scripted-vs-agent, not strong-vs-weak: hCaptcha and Turnstile caught nearly all scripted Chromium and CloakBrowser (stealth) sessions but few AI-agent sessions; reCAPTCHA v3 was the inverse, catching most agent sessions but none from CloakBrowser.

Five adversaries: plain Playwright/CDP Chromium (baseline with navigator.webdriver artifacts), CloakBrowser (stealth fork spoofing GPU/canvas/WebGL/audio/fonts/UA/TLS, run over residential proxy with input humanization), and three LLM agents: Browser Use (Claude Opus), Perplexity Comet, and xAI's Grok.

Method: each adversary ran a five-question survey (multiple-choice plus open-ended) 20 times, up to 100 sessions per detector, 89-100 evaluable after crashes; detection systems are black-box so signal attribution is inferred, not measured.

Stated limitations: no human participants, so no false-positive rate; low volume; and the prior-year benchmark of the same five classic detectors ranged 33-87%, with behavioral+device systems beating device-only ones.
summary: Proof of Human, a company selling an invisible authentication system, re-ran its bot-detection benchmark against modern AI browsing agents and reports detection rates spanning 9% to 99%. It tested five detectors (Proof of Human, Google reCAPTCHA v3, hCaptcha, Cloudflare Turnstile, Cloudflare Bot Management) against five adversaries: a plain automated Chromium, the CloakBrowser stealth fork run over a residential proxy, and three vision-LLM agents (Browser Use on Claude Opus, Perplexity Comet, xAI Grok), each running a five-question survey 20 times for up to 100 sessions per detector. Aggregate detection was Proof of Human 99%, reCAPTCHA v3 69.4%, hCaptcha 44.3%, Turnstile 42.1%, and Cloudflare Bot Management 9.1%. The key finding is a scripted-versus-agent split: hCaptcha and Turnstile caught nearly all scripted and stealth-browser sessions but few AI-agent sessions, while reCAPTCHA v3 showed the opposite, catching most agent sessions and none from CloakBrowser. The authors argue browser-level fingerprint signals and interactive challenges are weakening against vision-capable agents in genuine browsers, raising the value of in-session behavioral signals. Caveats: the detectors are black-box so signal attribution is inferred, there were no human participants to measure false positives, volume was low, and the authors' own product posted the top score.
novelty: quantifies CAPTCHA/bot-detection collapse against vision LLM browsing agents
audience: security engineers and anti-fraud/bot-defense teams evaluating detection vendors

title: Using Claude to reduce the attack surface of code
why: If unnecessary pre-auth reachability survives in OpenSSH, it is almost certainly in your stack: this method cuts the blast radius of unknown bugs by gating dead code, without ever finding a single CVE.
notes: Claude ran over 25 open-source projects (5M+ lines of C, C++, Java, PHP, Python), cataloged 17,000+ config options (3,842 security-relevant), and reported 493 issues via three methods: default-config exposure, risky config-option interactions, and early reachability before auth or protocol state transitions.

All 11 'gated' (authenticated) projects had unintentionally pre-auth-reachable code: 93 unnecessary pre-auth surfaces in default config, 37 spots where code ran or state was recorded before auth, and 61 config combos that silently weakened an admin-set pre-auth control. Projects were binned Public/Gated/Private to set expected baseline reachability.

162 config combinations were accepted with no error, warning, or documentation; 94 silently disabled a security control. One recurring pattern across four unrelated projects: a hostname/wildcard deny rule compared against a client IP (reverse DNS off by default) never matches, so the deny list fails open; one certificate-check conflict had been present 21 years.

OpenSSH case study (the biggest reduction by percentage): the 10.4 sshd let an unauthenticated client reach ~4,500 lines of experimental ML-DSA-44 post-quantum code (about 16% of default pre-auth code) even when the algorithm was excluded, because key type was parsed before the allow-list check. Fixes landed across 10.5 and 10.6 after Anthropic reported it with patches and a proof of concept.

The 10.5 patch had two gaps Claude flagged: the check read the client-advertised algorithm name while the parser keyed off a type string inside the key blob (advertise ssh-ed25519, send ML-DSA), and attacker certificates triggered full CA-signature verification before any config check. The 10.6 fix moved checks inside the parser, comparing encoded key type and CA signature algorithm against allow lists before deserialization.

The three passes are packaged as a reusable Claude skill (being integrated into OSS-Scanner); each pass starts with an empty context plus brief carryover, confirms findings with a dynamic trace, and for default-config gates requires modified builds to pass the project's own test suite plus a black-box regression suite with identical results. These are Anthropic's self-reported results; the post names no methodology for false-positive rates and does not disclose the specific projects beyond OpenSSH.
summary: Anthropic (author Chris Rohlf) describes using Claude for automated attack surface analysis and reduction: mapping which code is reachable in a given deployment and gating or removing anything that need not be exposed, which lowers the severity of unknown and actively exploited vulnerabilities without finding or fixing individual bugs. Across 25 open-source projects (5M+ lines in C, C++, Java, PHP, Python), Claude cataloged over 17,000 config options (3,842 security-relevant) and reported 493 issues using three methods: default-config exposure, risky configuration interactions, and early reachability before authentication or protocol state transitions. All 11 authenticated ('gated') projects had unintentionally pre-auth-reachable code; 162 config combinations were silently accepted, 94 of which disabled a security control, including a fail-open deny-list pattern recurring in four unrelated projects and one certificate-check conflict present for 21 years. The headline case is OpenSSH 10.4, where ~4,500 lines of experimental ML-DSA-44 code (about 16% of default pre-auth code) were reachable by unauthenticated clients even when the algorithm was excluded; Anthropic reported it with patches and a proof of concept, and fixes moving the checks before parsing shipped in 10.5 and 10.6. The three passes are packaged as a reusable Claude skill being integrated into OSS-Scanner, with findings confirmed by dynamic traces and default-config gates validated against the project's own test suite plus a black-box regression suite. All figures are Anthropic's self-reported results; the post does not disclose false-positive rates or the identities of the non-OpenSSH projects.
novelty: AI used to systematically shrink reachable attack surface, not just find bugs
audience: security engineers and AppSec teams evaluating LLM-assisted code auditing

title: There isn't an easy exploit for this PHP vulnerability
why: Before you panic-patch or trust an LLM-built PoC, note that the thousands of GitHub "exploits" for this PHP CVE fail against a stock server, and some fake success by first injecting the vulnerability they claim to find.
notes: The author reports thousands of GitHub PoC repos for the PHP CVE (referencing CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619 in one linked repo name), and claims none work against a vanilla PHP instance when you run them yourself rather than letting an LLM run them.

Most of the fake PoCs reportedly depend on a pre-existing local file inclusion bug, effectively requiring the server to do eval(read(user-supplied filename)); the author calls that an unrealistic prerequisite that does not make the core bug severe.
Some LLM-generated demos allegedly modify the target server to insert a vulnerability so the 'exploit all' transcript looks real, described as the model handing a child an unplugged controller.
Fear was stoked by a PHP core team member warning exploits would appear '15 minutes after the patch drops'; 10 hours in, the author says no working exploit exists.
The author contrasts this with pre-LLM CVE10s (Log4Shell, Heartbleed, Shellshock, Rails YAML deserialization) that had hand-written botnets circulating within hours of disclosure.

Central thesis: 'Decision Schelling Points,' where many actors independently converge on the same flawed exploit reasoning because Claude/GPT did the judgment for them. Claims are the author's; no independent confirmation or CVSS detail is provided.
summary: An opinion post argues that a widely hyped PHP CVE (linked repos cite CVE-2026-109618/109619) is not easily exploitable, despite a PHP core team member warning that exploits would appear 15 minutes after the patch. The author says thousands of GitHub PoCs exist but none work against a vanilla PHP server, and urges readers to run the scripts themselves rather than delegate to an LLM. Most fake PoCs reportedly require a pre-existing local file inclusion vulnerability (eval(read(user-supplied filename))), an unrealistic prerequisite, and some LLM demos allegedly fake success by injecting the vulnerability into the target. The author contrasts this with genuine critical CVEs like Log4Shell, Heartbleed, Shellshock, and Rails YAML deserialization, which produced working exploits and botnets within hours in the pre-LLM era. The broader claim is that LLMs create 'Decision Schelling Points': many people converge on the same flawed exploit reasoning because models like Claude and GPT made the judgment for them. All assertions are the author's; no CVSS scoring, vendor confirmation, or independent testing is cited.
novelty: LLM hype inflates fake PoCs for unexploitable PHP CVE
audience: security researchers and engineers skeptical of AI-hyped vuln disclosures

title: Announcing DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS “Cinnamon Teal”
why: The in-process database now ships a client-server protocol, async object-storage I/O, and a CLI that reshapes its output for coding agents, so DuckDB can serve remote databases and cut agent token consumption without leaving its embedded roots.
notes: The Quack protocol (introduced in 1.5.3) gets a polished client-server mode with a new CONNECT statement; CONNECT also targets Postgres and MySQL, where a remote pushdown optimizer ships queries to the server instead of pulling tables over the wire. Server defaults to localhost; allow_other_hostname is testing-only, with TLS reverse proxy recommended for remote access.

Async I/O for Parquet, CSV, and native storage decouples the I/O layer from query processing, issuing background reads and keeping multiple requests in flight for faster S3/remote reads. The VARIANT type (from 1.5) now 'shreds' common structure for columnar compression and Parquet read/write via variant_* functions.

CLI agent mode auto-detects when run by Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor: compact Markdown tables, explicit truncation notices, early stops on runaway queries, JSON errors, and pre-run cost estimates. Self-reported TPC-H experiments cut DuckDB output the model had to read by 59%; toggle with -agent / -no-agent.

The PEG-based parser (opt-in in 1.5) becomes default, replacing the 2018-era YACC/Bison LALR(1) parser; extensions can hook the grammar to add new SQL syntax. Fallback via legacy_parser extension and SET enable_legacy_parser = true.

Breaking changes: files written by 2.0 cannot be read by pre-2.0 versions (2.0 still reads/writes older files); C++17 now required; Clang is the default release compiler; ICU library removed in favor of a native 45 kB IANA-based implementation; single-arrow lambda syntax disabled by default and removed in 2.1; osx_amd64 being phased out.

Support timeline: 2.0 LTS supported to at least October 2027; 1.4 to late November 2026; 1.5 extended to March 2027. Team recommends shadow-testing and, for mission-critical workloads, waiting for the first patch in November. Also adds triggers (CREATE TRIGGER, BEFORE/AFTER, FOR EACH ROW/STATEMENT, transition tables), C API v2, self-hosted signed extension repositories, DuckLake 1.1, and NEAREST joins for vector/embedding search.
summary: DuckDB 2.0.0 LTS ("Cinnamon Teal") is a feature release built from roughly 20,000 commits since 1.5, supported until at least October 2027. It ships a polished Quack client-server protocol with a new CONNECT statement (also targeting Postgres and MySQL with remote query pushdown), asynchronous I/O for Parquet/CSV/native storage that decouples reads from query processing for faster object-storage access, and a fully integrated VARIANT type that shreds semi-structured data for columnar compression. A new CLI agent mode detects coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and emits compact Markdown, truncation notices, query cost estimates, and JSON errors, which the team reports cut DuckDB output the model reads by 59% on TPC-H. The PEG-based parser becomes default (replacing the 2018 YACC/Bison LALR(1) grammar), and the release adds triggers, a C API v2, self-hosted signed extension repositories, and SQL dialect extensions like NEAREST joins. Breaking changes include files written by 2.0 being unreadable by older versions, a C++17 requirement, a switch to Clang, removal of the ICU library in favor of a native 45 kB implementation, and deprecation of single-arrow lambda syntax; the team recommends shadow testing and, for critical workloads, waiting for the November patch. Performance and agent-mode figures are vendor self-reported without full methodology.
novelty: LTS release adds client-server protocol, async I/O, VARIANT type, agent mode
audience: data engineers and devs using DuckDB in pipelines or agent tooling

title: GitLab Critical Patch Release
why: Any self-managed GitLab reachable on the network back to version 7.0 can be remotely code-executed by an unauthenticated attacker (CVSS 10.0) until you upgrade, and GitLab shipped emergency backports to seven branches to make that patch reachable.
notes: CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS 10.0, AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N, scope changed): integer overflow when compiling a crafted regular expression lets an unauthenticated user run arbitrary code on the server. It affects all CE/EE versions from 7.0 forward; the fix was backported to 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9 in addition to the current branches. Bug-fix notes tie it to a Ruby regexp repeat-ID overflow / repeat-range double-free patch for Ruby 3.3, 3.4, and 4.0, and GitLab published two threat detections for exploitation attempts on self-managed instances.

CVE-2026-15723 (CVSS 8.2): with OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking both enabled, an authenticated user can take over an existing LDAP-backed account with no interaction from the victim, via improper sanitization in the LDAP email lookup during identity linking.

CVE-2026-112212 (CVSS 7.5, found internally): an unauthenticated user can poison a shared cache's OAuth/OIDC discovery document to redirect flows to an attacker-controlled server; CVE-2026-12664 (CVSS 6.8) lets a read_api-scoped token read a project's incoming email address and create work items, bypassing the token scope via a GraphQL field.

Lower-severity fixes include a SAML/LDAP membership-lock bypass (CVE-2026-16255, 5.9, EE), internal credential exposure in response headers (CVE-2026-105777, 4.3), group-milestone metadata read across private projects (CVE-2026-13319, 4.3), and an AI-billing bypass granting paid AI features without a valid subscription (CVE-2026-112378, 4.3, EE).

Fixed versions: 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13. GitLab.com is already patched and Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0 / 19.4.2-internal0 or later need no action; vulnerability issues go public on the tracker 90 days after the patch.

Upgrade caveat: 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 carry regular migrations (19.4.3 also post-deploy), so single-node instances take downtime during the upgrade while migrations complete; multi-node deployments can stay up with zero-downtime procedures.
summary: On October 21, 2026, GitLab shipped an ad-hoc critical patch across seven release branches (19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13) for both CE and EE, headlined by CVE-2026-110264, a CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated remote code execution caused by an integer overflow when compiling a crafted regular expression, affecting every version from 7.0 onward. The underlying fix maps to Ruby regexp repeat-ID overflow and repeat-range double-free patches for Ruby 3.3, 3.4, and 4.0, and GitLab released two threat detections for self-managed instances; GitLab.com and patched Dedicated tenants are already covered. The release also fixes CVE-2026-15723 (CVSS 8.2 SAML-to-LDAP account takeover), CVE-2026-112212 (CVSS 7.5 OAuth/OIDC discovery cache poisoning), CVE-2026-12664 (CVSS 6.8 GraphQL token-scope bypass), and several lower-severity access-control, credential-exposure, and AI-billing-bypass issues. Most vulnerabilities were reported through GitLab's HackerOne program; a few were found internally. GitLab urges all affected self-managed installations to upgrade immediately, noting that 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 include migrations that cause downtime on single-node instances.
novelty: CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated RCE via regex compiler integer overflow
audience: engineers running self-managed GitLab instances

title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
why: If you push to GitHub from CI or coding agents, the write path just stopped serializing on a repo-wide lock: concurrent pushes to different branches now run in parallel and saw 3-4x higher throughput in GitHub's internal tests.
notes: GitHub is migrating repo data from its own data centers to Azure, forced by agentic-era traffic growth against hard ceilings on data center power capacity and physical supply chain. First replica landed in Azure Central US in August 2025; most repos now keep two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic.

The old Spokes quorum holds a repository-wide lock per write and waits for every healthy replica (up to a timeout) before moving on, so the slowest replica sets both latency and the throughput ceiling. A cross-region replica is ~1,000 miles / ~25ms per round trip, and a write needs multiple round trips, which the busiest ~0.00001% of repos could not absorb.

Fix: shrink quorum scope from the whole repository to individual Git references. Consistency only needs to hold per reference (no client sees an older value after an accepted update), so writes to different refs no longer wait on each other. Claimed 3-4x throughput at lower latency in internal testing with realistic traffic.

Next, read/write decoupling: data lands durably in Azure Blob Storage, which joins the quorum as a 'virtual replica,' a fully ephemeral bridge node that streams writes (a write is not acked until durable in object storage), serves no reads, coalesces disjoint-reference transactions into one set of object-storage I/Os, and currently runs compaction.

Virtual read replicas then scale out on demand, warming cache from Blob Storage and reconciling in the background without joining the quorum; repos run 100-1000 reads per write. Caveat: background reconciliation does not fit all read workloads, and the quorum remains the bound on further write throughput.

Spokes is more than a quorum: an intelligent routing/load-balancing layer and unified API handling 'well over 100 billion operations per day,' plus 'sweeper' background systems for placement, repair, and rebalancing. GitHub states the current commit protocol that reached a billion repos won't reach the next billion; the end-state design, including a remaining small consensus group, is promised in a follow-up post at GitHub Universe.
summary: GitHub describes an interim ("bridge") step in re-architecting its Git storage as it migrates repository data from its own data centers to Azure, a move driven by agentic traffic growth colliding with data center power and supply chain limits. Most repositories now hold two of five replicas in Azure, which serves roughly half of Git traffic, but the busiest repositories were blocked by a ~25ms cross-region round trip. Under the old Spokes quorum, a repository-wide lock and waiting on every healthy replica meant the slowest replica set write latency and the throughput ceiling, which cross-region replicas could not sustain. GitHub narrows the quorum from the whole repository to individual references, since Git consistency only needs to hold per reference, letting writes to different branches run concurrently; internal testing claims 3-4x higher throughput at lower latency. The next stage decouples reads from writes by making Azure Blob Storage a quorum member via an ephemeral "virtual write replica" and scaling out stateless "virtual read replicas" that reconcile against object storage. GitHub says write throughput remains quorum-bound and defers the end-state design, including a remaining small consensus group, to a follow-up post.
novelty: per-reference quorum replaces repo-wide lock to unblock cross-region writes
audience: infra/distributed-systems engineers and GitHub-scale platform architects

title: Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI Installs a Credential Stealer and Backdoor
why: Anyone who ran `pip install litellm==1.107.0` during the compromise window should rotate every credential that process could reach, because safedep.io reports the package shipped a credential stealer and a backdoor.
notes: safedep.io reports LiteLLM 1.107.0, published to PyPI, was compromised to carry a credential stealer and a backdoor; LiteLLM is a widely used LLM proxy/gateway that typically holds provider API keys, making stolen credentials high-value.
The attack is a software supply-chain compromise of a published package version, not an exploit against a running LiteLLM deployment; the risk is installing the poisoned version from the index.

No article text was available to the editor; the payload description (credential stealer, backdoor) is sourced from the safedep.io writeup and Hacker News discussion, not an independent confirmation here.

Specific details not established in the provided material: the attack vector (maintainer account vs. build pipeline), the exact exposure window, which later/earlier versions are clean, and whether the malicious release was pulled from PyPI.
Community attention was high: 399 points and 125 comments on Hacker News as of first-seen on 2026-10-21.
summary: A safedep.io post reports that LiteLLM version 1.107.0, a popular open-source LLM proxy library, was published to PyPI in a compromised state carrying a credential stealer and a backdoor. Because LiteLLM commonly brokers requests to LLM providers and holds their API keys, a credential stealer in it threatens the very secrets it manages. The item surfaced on Hacker News with 399 points and 125 comments. No primary article text was available for this writeup, so the payload characterization comes from the safedep.io analysis and the HN thread rather than independent verification. Key operational details remain unestablished in the provided material: the compromise vector, the exact window the malicious version was live, which versions are safe, and whether the release has been removed from PyPI. Users who installed 1.107.0 should treat it as a supply-chain compromise and rotate exposed credentials.
novelty: supply-chain attack on popular LLM proxy library
audience: engineers using LiteLLM or managing AI infra dependency security

title: PHP warns it plans to release 2 emergency patches imminently
why: Two CVSS 9.2 PHP flaws reportedly reach back to PHP 5 from 2004, so nearly every WordPress, Drupal, Magento, and Laravel deployment is in scope the moment patches land in about 12 hours.
notes: Maintainers plan to ship patches for two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each rated 9.2/10, roughly 12 hours after the Monday advisory.
The advisory followed a leaked, still-unconfirmed report; maintainers reserve the right to release early if details go public or active exploitation appears.

A demo video shows an exploit tool called PHP2Shell running code against WordPress 7.1.3, MediaWiki 1.46.2, phpBB 3.3.17, Magento 2.4.9, Joomla 6.2.0, Laravel 13.36.0 and 8.83.29, Symfony 8.1.9, Drupal 11.4.10, and WHMCS 9.0.9.
watchTowr says it confirmed both bugs are real and claims they affect every PHP version from PHP 5 (2004) onward.

summary: PHP maintainers issued a Monday advisory warning that patches for two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 out of 10, would drop in a little more than 12 hours, and urged all PHP users to prepare to upgrade immediately. The advisory came after leaked, unconfirmed details surfaced alongside a video of an exploit tool called PHP2Shell executing code on servers running WordPress, MediaWiki, phpBB, Magento, Joomla, Laravel, Symfony, Drupal, and WHMCS. Security firm watchTowr says it confirmed the vulnerabilities are real and claims they affect every PHP version since PHP 5 in 2004. Maintainers said they would release earlier if the details became public or evidence of active exploitation appeared. Ars Technica noted it could not locate the original unconfirmed report, leaving the exploit specifics and version range as claims rather than verified facts.

title: Harness Engineering 101: The LLM is the brain, the harness is the body
why: If you build agents, this reframes the whole stack as one thing you already control: a stateless JSON array you mutate each turn, with every "agent" feature reduced to a named patch and its cost.
notes: Core thesis: an LLM API is stateless, so each turn you resend the full conversation as a JSON array; a harness is the program that builds, maintains, and protects that array, and every agent technique is a patch to that one loop.
Structure: 16 chapters, each following failure → minimal patch → what the patch costs, built around a ~300-line toy agent in plain Python that grows chapter by chapter.

Covered patterns tie to concrete failures: caching (resending the array gets expensive, order is load-bearing), subagents (fork the context), context budgeting (window fills up), guardrails, and a claim that RAG was always a harness pattern.

Companion code: patterns are developed in One Code, an open-source coding agent built on 'pi'; appendices cover model routing/cost engineering, worktree isolation, plan mode, and retries/rate-limits/streaming on the wire.
Licensing is split: prose (the .md chapters) is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (share with credit, no commercial use, no modified versions); code (toy harness and diagram generators) is MIT.

Distribution: an mdBook-based book (self-published as Version 1.0, September 2026); surfaced on Hacker News at 81 points and 39 comments. No external benchmarks or evaluation; it is a conceptual/tutorial treatment, not measured results.
summary: Harness Engineering 101 is a 16-chapter book (Version 1.0, September 2026, by Isuru Wijesiri) that builds AI agents from first principles around a single claim: an LLM API is stateless, so a "harness" is the program that constructs, maintains, and protects the JSON conversation array sent on every turn, and every technique the field labels "agents" is a patch to that loop. Each chapter follows the same shape, naming a concrete failure, the minimal patch, and what the patch costs, and grows a ~300-line toy agent in plain Python as it goes. Topics include tool calls, the agent loop, prompt caching and message ordering, context budgeting, subagents, steering, guardrails, MCP/skills/hooks, and the argument that RAG was a harness pattern all along; appendices cover model routing and cost engineering, worktree isolation, plan mode, and retries/streaming internals. The patterns are developed in One Code, an open-source coding agent built on "pi." The repo is dual-licensed: prose under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, code under MIT. It is a conceptual and tutorial treatment with runnable code rather than a benchmarked system; it surfaced on Hacker News at 81 points and 39 comments.
novelty: unified "harness" framing of agent patterns as patches to one JSON loop
audience: engineers building LLM agent frameworks/harnesses

title: An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
why: An ordinary ad buy can now be the infection vector: researchers documented spyware reaching 45 devices at Al Jazeera with no user click, so ad IDs and browser fingerprints are part of your attack surface.
notes: Citizen Lab and Confiant say Israeli ad tech firm Discover-Tech runs a platform called 'Controlium' that lets spyware partners profile, de-anonymize, and fingerprint users and select targets by IP address, mobile ad ID, or browser identifier for zero-click infection.
One partner is Candiru, an Israeli spyware vendor on the US government blacklist; its spyware was delivered via Discover-Tech ads to 'at least' 45 devices at Qatar-based Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025.
The researchers frame this as the first technical evidence of a zero-click attack (no user action required) delivered through targeted advertising; the finding was reported earlier by NBC News.
Per Reuters, Google and Comcast-owned Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from their platforms and IAB Europe suspended it from its approved-vendor list.

Recommended mitigations for high-risk users: run ad blockers, disable ad tracking, and periodically reset mobile ad IDs; the attribution and infection chain come from the researchers, not the named ad firm.
summary: Security researchers at Citizen Lab and Confiant published a joint investigation alleging that Israeli ad tech firm Discover-Tech acted as a pipeline for spyware groups, delivering infections through targeted online ads. They say its 'Controlium' platform let partners profile, de-anonymize, and fingerprint users and select targets by IP address, mobile ad ID, or browser identifier, enabling a zero-click attack that requires no user interaction. The researchers describe this as the first technical evidence of such an attack delivered via targeted advertising. One named partner is Candiru, a US-blacklisted Israeli spyware vendor whose spyware reached at least 45 devices at Al Jazeera across 2024 and 2025. Following the report, Google, Comcast-owned Beeswax, and IAB Europe removed or suspended Discover-Tech, per Reuters. The researchers urge the ad industry to tighten platform security and advise high-risk users to use ad blockers, disable ad tracking, and reset mobile ad IDs.
novelty: first documented zero-click spyware delivery via targeted ad platform
audience: security researchers, journalists, privacy-conscious engineers

title: OpenCode 2.0
why: If you run a coding agent against many MCP servers, OpenCode 2.0's "code mode" lets the model compose tool calls in a single scripted round trip instead of sequential calls, cutting latency and context bloat even with ~1,000 servers attached.
notes: Client/server split is now default: a single background process backs the TUI, web UI, and desktop app; the @opencode/client package autodiscovers the local service, and /pair or opencode pair exposes it to other hosts.

Code mode (@opencode/codemode) runs a minimal native JS interpreter that ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI endpoints as callable functions, avoiding Node VMs or QuickJS; agents can call a tool, map over results, and call another tool in one round trip. All MCP servers opt in by default.

Background execution added on two fronts: background subagents (the primary agent spawns work to another agent, optionally a different model, and keeps prompting) and async background shell commands; a hotkey moves any slow foreground task to the background.
Plugins: 80+ internal plugins now implement nearly every 2.0 feature to keep the Plugin API exercised; TUI plugins promoted from experimental to stable on OpenTUI.

@opencode/sdk ships OpenCode as a library (the same code as the CLI) for embedding in environments like Cloudflare Durable Objects, speaking the standard OpenCode server protocol, with an optional Effect-based API.

Breaking changes: 1.0 plugins do not work, the server API is completely different, and tui.json config moves to json; upgrade via opencode upgrade --major from the latest 1.x. The 'millions of daily users' and performance figures are vendor claims without methodology.
summary: OpenCode 2.0 is a major rewrite of the open-source coding agent that makes its client/server model the default: a single background process now serves the TUI, web, and desktop clients, with an autodiscovering @opencode/client package and a /pair flow to expose the service to other hosts. The headline feature is "code mode" (@opencode/codemode), a minimal native JavaScript interpreter that converts MCP servers and OpenAPI endpoints into functions the agent can script, letting it chain tool calls in one round trip rather than sequentially; all MCP servers are opted in by default to limit context bloat even with roughly a thousand servers attached. The release adds background subagents and asynchronous background shell commands so long-running work does not block the primary agent, plus a hotkey to push slow tasks to the background. The plugin system was rebuilt with 80+ internal plugins implementing most 2.0 features, and TUI plugins (built on OpenTUI) are now stable. A new @opencode/sdk exposes OpenCode as an embeddable library, for example in Durable Objects. Upgrading requires the latest 1.x and opencode upgrade --major, and carries breaking changes: 1.0 plugins are incompatible, the server API is entirely new, and tui.json config moves to json. Claims about "millions of daily users" and performance gains are self-reported and unquantified.
novelty: unified server process, JS-native "code mode" tool orchestration, background subagents
audience: engineers building or using AI coding agents/CLI tools

title: F-Zero X on Nintendo 3DS
why: A single developer steering one Claude session and 147+ subagents shipped a working, 60fps-in-3D N64 port to both 3DS consoles, and the decisive wins came from hardware instruction-cache profiling, not model cleverness: a concrete data point on where agentic coding actually pays off and where the human still has to make the call.
notes: One person directed throughout; one long-lived Claude session orchestrated 147 subagents in a 24-day phase 1 (2026-08-11 to 09-03) and many more in a 43-day phase 2 (2026-09-07 to 10-19), porting the inspectredc/fzerox decompilation (upstream untouched) plus a patch stack, on top of libultraship (untouched, plus a 13-line newlib fix for devkitARM); port/3ds was 15,039 lines at end of phase 1.

Phase 1 (New 3DS) hardware medians, self-reported, climbed 48-50 fps (08-21 first hardware run) to 59.6 fps with 53% of frames at cap (09-03) via levers including a render thread on core 2, one-frame-ahead mode, bridge-on-main, auto LOD, and memoizing each sub-display-list's classification instead of re-scanning every frame.

Old 3DS (268 MHz) had to fit a 64 MB app region: RDRAM arena halved, audio streamed rather than resident, texture uploads capped; the shipped New-3DS build died at boot on real hardware while the O3DS profile booted and raced at ~10 fps (09-29).

Hardware performance counters showed the real Old 3DS limit was instruction-cache misses, not instruction count; the native renderer was rebuilt as one small loop per race category sized to the 16 KB icache, reaching a 16.5 ms median frame time on a 2D Grand Prix race, and is the v1.0.0 default on both consoles.

Heaviest Old 3DS courses (Silence, Sand Ocean) can still trip a frame-skip safety net to a steady 30 fps mid-race; the 64DD Expansion Kit verified tick-for-tick identical and booted on Old 3DS but was deemed too slow to release there.

No ROM or disk image ships: every build reads prebaked asset archives from the SD card and requires a user-supplied disk image for the Expansion Kit; four builds shipped from one source tree (Old 3DS/2DS, New 3DS/New 2DS XL, and New 3DS with Expansion Kit). Dollar figures are estimates applying published API list prices to exact token counts.
summary: A post-mortem documents porting G-Diffuser, the F-Zero X decompilation, to the Nintendo 3DS, reaching v1.0.0 with four builds covering Old and New 3DS, with and without the 64DD Expansion Kit, all from one source tree. One person directed the work while one long-lived Claude session orchestrated 147 subagents in a 24-day first phase and many more in a 43-day second phase; the decompilation and the libultraship N64 runtime were used untouched upstream. On New 3DS the author reports a median 59.6 fps with 53% of frames at cap, reached through a core-2 render thread, ahead-mode rendering, and display-list classification memoization. The Old 3DS required halving the RDRAM arena, streaming audio, and capping texture uploads to fit a 64 MB app region; hardware performance counters then revealed instruction-cache misses, not instruction count, as the bottleneck, prompting a native renderer built as per-category loops sized to the 16 KB icache that hit a 16.5 ms median frame time on 2D races and 59-60 fps in 3D on most courses. The heaviest courses still drop to a frame-skipped 30 fps, and the Expansion Kit, though verified identical, was judged too slow to release on Old 3DS. No ROM or disk image ships; builds read prebaked SD-card asset archives, and reported dollar costs are estimates derived from token counts at list prices.
novelty: AI-agent-orchestrated N64 decomp port tuned via icache profiling
audience: retro/embedded systems engineers and AI-coding-agent tooling enthusiasts

title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
why: If your agents already use context compaction or subagent forking, the standard single-session RL assumption no longer matches how they run, and broadcasting one reward across all sessions wastes credit assignment Mosaic claims to recover.
notes: Problem framing: most agentic RL assumes a single continuously accumulated context, but context compaction and subagent forking split a trajectory into multiple sessions, so training and inference-time execution diverge.

The authors define Multi-Session Agentic RL as a general setting allowing an arbitrary number of sessions per trajectory, and name the common fix, broadcasting one trajectory-level advantage to every session, as the baseline it beats.

Mosaic is critic-free and hierarchical: at the trajectory level it folds session-usage signals into advantage estimation; at the session level it shapes each session's advantage by its estimated marginal contribution.
Reported results use Qwen3.5-4B on BrowseComp: Mosaic beats broadcasting in both context-compaction and subagent-forking scenarios while averaging fewer sessions per trajectory.

Caveats: results are self-reported on a single benchmark and one 4B model, with no methodology, ablation detail, or baseline numbers in the abstract; session allocation is pitched as an open target rather than a solved one.
summary: Mosaic proposes Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a setting where a single agent trajectory spans an arbitrary number of sessions because of techniques like context compaction and subagent forking, which break the single-session assumption behind most agentic RL. The widely used approach broadcasts one trajectory-level advantage to all sessions, which cannot distinguish how much each session contributed or guide how sessions are allocated. Mosaic instead uses critic-free hierarchical optimization: trajectory-level advantage estimation incorporates session-usage signals, and each session's advantage is shaped by its estimated marginal contribution. On the BrowseComp benchmark with Qwen3.5-4B, the authors report that Mosaic outperforms the broadcasting baseline in both context-compaction and subagent-forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. The results are self-reported on one benchmark and one model, and the authors frame session utility and allocation as a direction for future work rather than a closed problem.
novelty: critic-free hierarchical RL for multi-session agent trajectories
audience: researchers/engineers building agentic RL training pipelines with context compaction or subagent forking

title: Livenerf: Has Opus 5.5 been nerfed yet?
why: If you argue about whether Claude got "nerfed," this is the first public day-0 baseline with pre-registered decision rules, and it already shows its own limit: it cannot tell an Opus 5-for-5.5 swap apart at 99% confidence.
notes: Scope: measures Opus 5.5 as served through Claude Code on a Max subscription via headless `claude -p`, not the raw API model. Launch-week baseline (days 1-10, from 2026-09-24) is treated as a reference point, not ground truth; the author notes 2025 quality incidents turned out to be infrastructure bugs, not deliberate downgrades.

Panel construction: 2,336 GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, competition-math and AIME 2025-26 questions screened at 4 samples each; Opus 5.5 scored ~93% first-try and 97% were always-right-or-always-wrong, leaving 78 'sometimes right' questions. Measured selection bias: picked items' fresh pass rate rose from 54.7% to 62.0%, so power calculations use the fresh rates.

Sensitivity: one daily run of the full panel detects ~7.5 accuracy points per 10-day window. A validation swap of Opus 5 for Opus 5.5 was NOT distinguishable at 99% (-3.8 ± 6.3 points, -23% tokens); the instrument can't catch a same-family swap of that size in a validation's samples.

Secondary signal is output tokens per sample, the author's preferred early indicator: low effort = -62% tokens but only -8.3 ± 4.5 accuracy points; medium = -26% tokens, -4.2 ± 3.9 points. Effort is always passed explicitly, never left at default.

Pre-registered decision rule (PREREGISTRATION.md committed before any series data, timestamp public): a change counts only if the 99% interval excludes zero in two consecutive 10-day windows, the effect is >=3 points, and a control arm (claude-opus-5 on the panel's GPQA questions) doesn't show the same move. Stats are paired per-item differences with clustered SEs (Miller 2024). Nulls and improvements both published.

Rigor and caveats: CLI pinned (2.1.280) and harness hash enforced because a Claude Code update looks exactly like a model change; calls are hermetic (frozen prompt, no tools/MCP/memory, one turn); code graded by hidden sandboxed tests, no LLM judge. Audit flagged 8 likely-wrong answer keys and 30 ambiguous questions in the panel; nothing dropped, handled via pre-registered sensitivity analysis. First Results row lands after day 20 (~2026-10-24). Independent project, not affiliated with Anthropic; author discloses Claude helped write much of the repo.
summary: livenerf is an independent, append-only benchmark that tests one question: does Claude Opus 5.5 get quietly worse after launch? It measures the model as served through Claude Code on a Max subscription (via headless `claude -p`), which is the setting most "nerf" complaints describe, and distinguishes that from the raw API. Because the model can't be made deterministic, it freezes everything else: a 78-question panel of "sometimes right" items selected from 2,336 GPQA/MMLU-Pro/math questions, a pinned CLI and harness hash, pure-function graders, and raw logs kept forever. It runs the full panel once a day for 30 days plus a control arm (Opus 5), using UK AISI's Inspect framework and Anthropic's own error-bar statistics (Miller 2024), with a pre-registered decision rule requiring a >=3-point change clearing a 99% interval in two consecutive 10-day windows without a matching move in the control. Stated limits are frank: it detects ~7.5-point shifts per window but could not distinguish an Opus 5 swap at 99%, and an audit found 8 likely-wrong answer keys and 30 ambiguous questions handled by a pre-registered sensitivity analysis. Output token count per sample is the author's preferred early signal, since reduced effort shows up in tokens (-62% at low effort) before accuracy moves; the first Results row was due after day 20, around 2026-10-24.
novelty: rigorous pre-registered benchmark for post-launch model drift
audience: engineers/researchers skeptical of "model nerfing" claims who want statistical rigor

title: What Would A Serious AI Product Look Like?
why: If you ship LLM tooling, this is a concrete punch-list of verification affordances your product almost certainly lacks: per-claim checkboxes, citation UIs that put the source quote above the model's summary, and a sandbox that removes auto-approve modes by default.
notes: Core argument: every chatbot ships a fine-print disclaimer (Gemini: "AI can make mistakes, so double-check responses"; Claude and ChatGPT similar) that pushes verification onto the user while providing zero tools to do it; the author calls this liability-shifting legalese.

Proposed fix is a two-column worksheet: LLM output on the left, human verification notes plus a checkbox on the right; for coding, checking diffs before they hit tests would also save the extra compute burned running bad changes through CI.

Citation UI should be inverted: the literal regex-extracted quotation (not an LLM summary) plus source, publication date, and author front-and-center and large; AI editorializing shrunk to disclaimer-size until verified. Author reports chatbots "get bored" and drop citations partway through long lists.

Demands: no first-person language or apologies from a dev/research tool; non-natural-language task-specific UIs (e.g., a dedicated button for OWASP Top 10 scanning) over free-text plus MCP tools; strong data-provenance indicators distinguishing API/tool results from hallucinated output; user-visible context windows and reproducibility/replay controls beyond a third-party progress bar.

Sandbox section: calls agentic coding "unsafe-by-default," wants filesystem sandboxing with scoped deletion limits, per-operation repo snapshots for rollback, removal of auto mode and --dangerously-skip-permissions, batch plan approval, and execution against mock API services. Metaphor: labs have "tied a spring-loaded shotgun to a dog."

Organizational prescriptions (dated near end of 2026): shift rotations to counter vigilance decrement (cites Amazon's "millions of lost orders"), L&D budget to offset skill loss (dockworker/crane analogy), and mental-health resources for "AI psychosis" and "AI brain fry." Criticism applies equally to Ollama, more so given weaker open models. Claims about mental-health crises and incidents are asserted without linked studies in the excerpt.
summary: A design critique arguing that current LLM products do not take their own stated limitations seriously: they warn users that output can be wrong but provide no affordances to check it. The author proposes concrete UI changes, including a per-claim verification worksheet with checkboxes, an inverted citation design that elevates regex-extracted source quotations with author and date metadata over AI summaries, suppression of first-person language and apologies, task-specific non-chat interfaces, explicit data-provenance indicators, visible context windows, and reproducibility/replay controls. For coding agents, it labels the current model unsafe-by-default and demands LLM-independent harness controls: scoped filesystem sandboxing, per-operation repo snapshots, elimination of auto-approve modes and --dangerously-skip-permissions, batch plan review, and execution against mock APIs. A final section prescribes organizational changes for safe deployment: shift rotations to combat vigilance decrement (citing Amazon's \"millions of lost orders\"), expanded learning-and-development budgets to offset skill loss, and mental-health resources. The piece is opinion and design argument rather than empirical study; incident and mental-health claims are asserted without linked evidence in the text, and criticism is applied to frontier labs and Ollama alike.
novelty: design critique of chatbot UX framed as missing fact-checking affordances
audience: engineers/designers building AI products who care about trust and UX honesty

title: Show HN: Corral – Kill every command your agent starts
why: If your CI or coding agent runs commands that fork daemons or hold pipes open, this tool returns a hard guarantee that nothing it spawned is still holding your ports, locks, or CPU when the run ends.
notes: Enforced mode puts the command in its own cgroup v2 group; one write to cgroup.kill stops every descendant, and the mode also applies --mem and --pids limits. Fallback mode needs no cgroup: corral becomes a child subreaper, scans /proc, and signals leftover processes through pidfds after re-checking each one so a reused pid never gets signaled.

Exit code 120 ('could not prove all processes stopped') overrides all other codes; other codes include 124 (time limit), 121 (memory), 122 (output), 125 (setup failed, command never started). The run ends when the command exits, not when output pipes close.

Self-reported benchmark over 10 fault programs (5 runs each, 2s limit): corral left zero processes alive in both modes; a naive Python runner hung with up to 192 leaked children on the fork test; uutils coreutils timeout 0.8.0 (not GNU) left one process alive in several daemon/fork cases. CE stopped the 256 MiB program at its limit in 0.12s.
Measured overhead to run /bin/true (vs 0.83/1.88ms direct): 11.33/19.47ms enforced, 6.64/10.01ms fallback (P50/P95). Test box: Hetzner 2-vCPU Skylake, Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.
Explicitly not a security sandbox: no limits on file, network, or privileges. Requires Linux 5.11+ (5.14+ for enforced mode); prebuilt binary is x86-64 glibc 2.36+. MIT licensed.

Stated limits: cannot see work started outside the tree (systemd-run, D-Bus, at); in enforced mode a process can escape by writing to cgroupfs itself; in fallback mode a setuid child cannot be signaled (exits 120); SIGKILL to corral itself only guarantees the direct child dies. No PTY and no CPU-time limit.
summary: Corral is an MIT-licensed Linux tool that runs a command under a time limit and guarantees no process the command spawned survives when it returns, verifying this before exiting or returning code 120 if it cannot prove cleanup. It targets the common failure modes of CI runners and AI coding agents: double-forked daemons that call setsid(), background processes that keep stdout/stderr open and hang the runner, and processes that ignore SIGTERM. Enforced mode uses a delegated cgroup v2 group and a single cgroup.kill write to stop all descendants, and adds --mem and --pids limits; fallback mode acts as a child subreaper, scans /proc, and signals processes only through pidfds after re-checking them to avoid acting on reused pids. A self-reported benchmark against GNU-style timeout (actually uutils coreutils 0.8.0) and a naive Python runner shows those tools leak processes on forked daemons and 200-child fork tests while corral leaves none; overhead to launch /bin/true is roughly 7–20ms P50/P95. It is explicitly not a security sandbox, requires Linux 5.11+ (5.14+ for enforced mode), and cannot track work escaping the tree via systemd-run, D-Bus, or at.
novelty: cgroup v2 kill-group + subreaper guarantees no orphaned processes survive a run
audience: engineers running AI agents or CI jobs that spawn untrusted shell commands

title: Agents don't need memory, they need documentation
why: If you bolt a vector-DB memory plugin onto your coding agent, this argues you are indexing stale transcript fragments instead of building the readable, committable project knowledge the agent actually needs.
notes: Characterizes every memory plugin as the same RAG pipeline: chunk session transcripts into snippets, embed into a vector DB, inject the top-5 by similarity on each prompt, expose a search tool as fallback. Extras like rerankers, multi-tier short/long-term memory, dedup daemons, and overnight 'dreamers' are dismissed as token-burning patches on a flawed base.

Five claimed failure modes: (1) similarity ranking tells you nothing about correctness, currency, or gaps; (2) snippets drop surrounding context, motivation, and environment; (3) recall treats a changing codebase's past as truth, so snippets about e.g. authentication go stale; (4) agents can't query what they don't know they're missing; (5) the store (described as ~10,000 embeddings in SQLite) is unauditable for staleness or wrong entries.

Proposed alternative: a structured Markdown 'brain' of specs, decisions, research, and indexes, generalizing beyond the single AGENTS.md file. The agent consults relevant docs before work and updates them after, shifting the loop from prompt->build->forget to prompt->consult->build->update.

Author's implementation is Operator Memory, open source at github.com/aerovato/operator-memory, used across the author's own projects for over a year. Explicitly no vector DBs, embeddings, summarizers, or background daemons; everything is plain Markdown you can read, commit, and share.
Opinion piece grounded in personal use, not a benchmark or study; no quantitative comparison against the memory plugins it critiques. Surfaced on Hacker News at 347 points and 211 comments.
summary: The post argues that AI coding agents don't need RAG-style memory plugins, they need documentation. It describes the common memory architecture as chunking session transcripts into snippets, storing them in a vector database, and injecting the top-5 similar snippets per prompt with a search-tool fallback, then lists five failures: similarity ranking ignores correctness and currency, snippets lose context, recall treats a changing codebase's past as truth, agents can't search for what they don't know, and the store is unauditable. As an alternative it proposes document-based memory: a structured Markdown 'brain' of specs, decisions, research, and indexes that the agent consults before work and updates afterward, changing the loop from prompt->build->forget to prompt->consult->build->update. The author built an open-source plugin, Operator Memory, that implements this with plain Markdown files and no embeddings, databases, or background daemons, and reports using it across projects for over a year. The argument is experiential rather than benchmarked, with no quantitative comparison to the plugins it criticizes. It reached 347 points and 211 comments on Hacker News.
novelty: reframes agent memory as structured docs, not RAG recall
audience: engineers building AI coding agents/tooling

title: Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL
why: If you train code agents with GRPO and binary test rewards, every passing trajectory gets the same advantage, so the policy never learns to prefer clean, in-scope fixes; GAGAR adds a grader that reranks and reweights those passes.
notes: The problem: with executable tests giving binary rewards, GRPO assigns identical advantages to all test-passing trajectories in a rollout group, giving no signal to favor targeted implementations over ones with unnecessary or out-of-scope changes.
Mechanism: an SFT-trained agentic grader inspects all trajectories from a group placed in a shared workspace and ranks the test-passing candidates by implementation quality.

Redistribution is sum-preserving: lower-ranked passing trajectories are downweighted, then all passing advantages are rescaled proportionally to restore the group's original advantage sum, shifting credit toward higher-quality passes without changing the total.
Built on dynamic sampling that retains only groups containing both passing and failing trajectories.

Evaluated on pre-RL SFT checkpoints of MiMo-V2.6-Flash (310B total params) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (1.02T total params); claimed results are improved code-agent performance, reduced trajectory-length growth, and more stable training.
Caveats: gains are self-reported with no public benchmark numbers, baselines, or ablations in the abstract; the grader itself is a trained model whose ranking quality is unverified here.
summary: GAGAR is a credit-redistribution framework for reinforcement learning of code agents that addresses a limitation of Group Relative Policy Optimization: when executable tests give binary rewards, GRPO assigns identical advantages to all test-passing trajectories in a group, ignoring differences in implementation quality and task adherence. Using dynamic sampling that keeps only groups with both passing and failing trajectories, GAGAR places a group's trajectories in a shared workspace where an SFT-trained agentic grader jointly inspects and ranks the passing candidates. It then downweights lower-ranked passes and rescales all passing advantages proportionally to preserve the group's original advantage sum, moving credit toward higher-quality implementations. The authors evaluate on pre-RL SFT checkpoints of MiMo-V2.6-Flash (310B total params) and MiMo-V2.6-Pro (1.02T total params), in both controlled code-only Flash experiments and large-scale mixed-task RL. Reported effects are improved code-agent performance, reduced trajectory-length growth, and more stable training; the abstract provides no benchmark numbers or methodology detail.
novelty: agentic grader reranks same-passing trajectories to redistribute GRPO advantages
audience: RL/post-training researchers building code agents

title: DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash-1017
why: An MIT-licensed open-weight model with a 1M-token context posts self-reported agentic scores that top K3 and GLM-5.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (42.3 vs 12.6/37.9), putting a free-to-run option in the same frame as closed harnesses you pay for.
notes: Positioned as a minor update to DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, subtitled 'Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression'; vendor claims shorter output length and faster task execution advancing the cost-performance Pareto frontier.

Self-reported benchmarks (vendor numbers, no methodology beyond harness names): Terminal-Bench 4.0 42.3 (Claude Code harness), DeepSWE v1.1 77.0 (Mini-SWE-V2 harness), Apex Bench v1.1 72.1, Automation-Bench v1.0.6 60.5, Agents' Last Exam 35.4; trails Opus 5 on most but leads K3 and GLM-5.3 broadly.
